name: Glycogen storage disease type IX (phosphorylase kinase deficiency)
aliases: Glycogen storage disease type IX (phosphorylase kinase)

clinicalPearls: Caused by deficiency of phosphorylase kinase, the multi-subunit enzyme that activates glycogen phosphorylase, so the functional block resembles GSD VI.
Collectively the most common of the hepatic glycogenoses, with marked genetic and clinical heterogeneity.
The X-linked liver form (PHKA2, GSD IXa) is the commonest subtype and is usually mild, often improving into adulthood.
Autosomal recessive subtypes include PHKB (liver and muscle) and PHKG2, the latter carrying a distinct risk of hepatic fibrosis and cirrhosis.
Typical presentation is childhood hepatomegaly, growth delay, mild motor delay and fasting ketotic hypoglycaemia.
Serum lactate and uric acid are usually normal, as in GSD VI, while transaminases, ketones and lipids may be raised.
Blood-cell enzyme assays can be misleading owing to tissue-specific subunit expression, so molecular genetics is preferred for diagnosis and subtyping.
Management is dietary, with avoidance of prolonged fasting, frequent carbohydrate intake and uncooked cornstarch; PHKG2 disease needs liver fibrosis surveillance.
reference.pathophysiology: Phosphorylase kinase is a large multi-subunit enzyme (alpha, beta, gamma catalytic and delta/calmodulin subunits) that phosphorylates and thereby activates glycogen phosphorylase, the enzyme that initiates glycogenolysis. The subunits are encoded by different genes with tissue-specific expression, which explains the genetic heterogeneity and the existence of liver-predominant, muscle-predominant and combined phenotypes. Reduced activation of hepatic phosphorylase impairs glycogen breakdown, causing hepatic glycogen accumulation with hepatomegaly and a tendency to fasting ketotic hypoglycaemia, while gluconeogenesis remains intact so lactate and urate handling are largely normal. The X-linked PHKA2 liver form is usually mild and self-limiting, whereas the autosomal recessive PHKG2 (gamma-2 catalytic subunit) form more often progresses to hepatic fibrosis and cirrhosis.
additionalDifferentials: Glycogen storage disease type VI (liver phosphorylase deficiency), which is clinically near-identical
Glycogen storage disease type III (debranching enzyme deficiency)
Glycogen storage disease type I (von Gierke), typically with lactic acidosis and hyperuricaemia
Glycogen storage disease type 0 (hepatic glycogen synthase deficiency)
Other causes of childhood hepatomegaly with transaminitis and fasting intolerance
additionalInvestigations: Molecular genetic testing of PHKA2, PHKB, PHKG2 (and PHKA1 for muscle forms) as the confirmatory approach
Controlled fasting studies documenting ketotic hypoglycaemia with normal lactate
Liver biochemistry, fasting lipids, lactate and urate
Abdominal ultrasound and, in PHKG2 disease, assessment of liver fibrosis (elastography or biopsy)
Phosphorylase kinase enzyme assay in erythrocytes or liver (interpreted cautiously given isoform effects)
Creatine kinase and, where muscle involvement is suspected, muscle-focused evaluation
redFlags: Symptomatic hypoglycaemia with seizures or reduced consciousness during illness or fasting
Signs of progressive liver disease (splenomegaly, coagulopathy, portal hypertension), particularly in PHKG2 disease
Faltering growth or failure to thrive
Evidence of hepatic fibrosis or cirrhosis on imaging or biopsy
reference.prognosis: The X-linked liver form generally has an excellent outcome, often improving through childhood and adolescence. The PHKG2 subtype carries a less certain prognosis with a genuine risk of progression to cirrhosis, so long-term hepatic surveillance is warranted.
pitfalls: Relying on erythrocyte enzyme assays, which can give false-negative or false-positive results because of tissue-specific isoforms
Assuming all GSD IX is mild and missing the fibrosis/cirrhosis risk of the PHKG2 subtype
Failing to distinguish it from the clinically identical GSD VI without genetic testing
Misclassifying it as GSD I when lactate and urate are in fact normal
references: Saudubray — Inborn Metabolic Diseases: Diagnosis and Treatment
Scriver — The Metabolic and Molecular Bases of Inherited Disease
management: Prevent fasting ketotic hypoglycaemia with frequent carbohydrate-rich feeds and uncooked cornstarch supplementation, avoiding prolonged fasts
Ensure adequate dietary protein to support intact gluconeogenesis and normal growth, guided by a metabolic dietitian
Institute an emergency regimen giving supplemental glucose during intercurrent illness, vomiting or reduced oral intake
Monitor growth, fasting glucose, ketones and liver biochemistry at regular intervals
Undertake long-term hepatic surveillance with ultrasound and fibrosis assessment by elastography, particularly in PHKG2 disease given its cirrhosis risk
Refer to metabolic medicine and hepatology, and offer genetic counselling and family screening given X-linked (PHKA2) and autosomal recessive inheritance
